rw: A deliverable is any tangible or intangible result the project must produce, such as a prototype, report or training session. Deliverables are agreed in scope and accepted by the client.

ww.A task that no one wants to do in the wh: A disliked task is not a deliverable. A deliverable is a defined output the project must produce, whether or not anyone enjoys the work behind it.
ww.A cost that the project must avoid becau: Deliverables add value rather than avoid cost. They are the planned outputs, such as a report, a product or a service, that the sponsor expects.
ww.A meeting held each week to review the p: A weekly progress meeting is a status or review activity, not a deliverable. Deliverables are the results produced, while meetings are just a way to coordinate work.

rw: A kickoff meeting launches the project by aligning the team and stakeholders on goals, roles, scope and schedule. A shared start reduces confusion and helps communication from day one.

ww.To collect payment from the customer aft: Collecting customer payment is a billing step that happens at or after delivery. A kickoff meeting happens at the start and focuses on aligning the project team.
ww.To train new customers on the product th: Training customers on a purchased product is customer support or onboarding. A kickoff meeting is an internal project launch for the team and stakeholders, not a product lesson.
ww.To end the project and review results wi: Ending the project and reviewing results with the client describes closing and a final review. A kickoff meeting happens at the beginning, not the end.

rw: A charter formally authorizes the project, names the project manager and states purpose, objectives and high-level scope. It gives the manager authority to use resources and is issued by the sponsor.

ww.A final bill sent to a customer when all: A final bill is an invoice sent for payment. A project charter is a start-up document that authorizes the project, not a billing record sent after work ends.
ww.A summary of the project's mistakes and: A summary of mistakes and who made them is not a charter. Lessons learned reviews are done at closing and should focus on improving processes, not blaming individuals.
ww.A list of tasks completed by the team, w: A list of completed tasks with dates and names is a progress or completion record. A charter is written before work begins to approve the project.

rw: The standard phases run initiate, plan, execute, monitor and close. Each phase builds on the one before it, and monitoring happens alongside execution until the project closes.

ww.Execute, close, plan, monitor, initiate: This order starts with executing and ends with initiating, which is backwards. Work cannot be executed before it is planned, and a project cannot be closed before it is started.
ww.Monitor, initiate, close, plan, execute: Beginning with monitoring and ending with execution is wrong. Monitoring tracks work already underway, so it cannot come first, and closing cannot come before execution.
ww.Close, execute, plan, initiate, monitor: Closing first and monitoring last is impossible. Closing finishes the project, so it must come at the end after the work has been executed and checked.

rw: In closing the work is finished, deliverables are handed over, contracts are closed and lessons learned are recorded. The client formally accepts the results and the team is released.

ww.The team is first formed and the goals a: Forming the team and choosing goals happens in initiation, at the start. Closing happens at the very end, after the work has been completed and delivered.
ww.The schedule is first drafted by the pro: Drafting the schedule is a planning task. Planning comes before execution, while closing is the last phase when the work is complete and results are handed over.
ww.Most of the work is done but the plan is: Doing most of the work while the plan is still changing describes the execution and monitoring phases. Closing starts only when the work is substantially complete.

rw: A status report summarizes progress to date, current issues and risks, and next steps. It keeps sponsors and stakeholders informed so they can decide or help early.

ww.A promotion for the team that finishes e: A promotion for a team that finishes early is a reward or incentive, not a report. A status report informs stakeholders on progress, not who gets rewarded.
ww.A list of staff birthdays for the whole: A list of staff birthdays is an HR or social record. A status report is a project communication tool that covers work progress, not personal dates.
ww.A contract for new work from a new clien: A contract for new work is a legal agreement setting terms and price. A status report does not commit anyone to new work, it only reports on current work.

rw: Regular communication keeps expectations aligned, builds trust and lets problems be spotted and resolved early. It also helps secure approvals and support throughout the life of the project.

ww.To avoid explaining problems to the spon: Regular communication does the opposite of avoiding problems. It surfaces issues early so they can be explained and solved before they grow into bigger issues for the sponsor.
ww.To keep stakeholders out of decisions an: Keeping stakeholders out of decisions weakens support and risks missing needs. Good project managers involve stakeholders so they stay informed, engaged and committed.
ww.To make team meetings longer for no real: Lengthening team meetings for no reason wastes time. Effective communication is planned, purposeful and sized to what stakeholders need to know.

rw: Resource allocation means assigning people, money, equipment and materials to project tasks. Good allocation matches skills and capacity to the work and avoids overload or idle resources.

ww.Deleting old project files to free up di: Deleting old project files is data management or housekeeping. Resource allocation is about assigning people, money and equipment to the tasks of a project.
ww.Setting prices for the project's product: Setting prices for products and services is a pricing decision made by marketing and management. Resource allocation decides who and what is used on project tasks.
ww.Selling the project's results to custome: Selling project results at a profit is a sales or revenue activity. Resource allocation happens within the project to supply the inputs needed to do the work.

rw: Rebalancing means moving some tasks from the overloaded member to the one with spare capacity. This protects quality and morale and uses the team's full capacity to meet deadlines.

ww.Leave the workload unchanged for the tea: Leaving the workload unchanged lets one person burn out while another sits idle, which lowers productivity and morale. A manager should act on an imbalance, not ignore it.
ww.Remove the overloaded member from the pr: Removing the overloaded member loses skills and makes the problem worse, because the remaining people must absorb even more work. It also punishes the person doing the most.
ww.Give the idle member a large cash bonus: A large cash bonus for an idle member rewards low output and does not fix the imbalance. Work should be redistributed so both people contribute fairly.

rw: Agile delivers work in short cycles, such as sprints, with frequent customer feedback. This lets teams adapt to changing needs and deliver usable results early and often.

ww.An approach that finishes all planning f: Finishing all planning first and never changing it describes a rigid, plan-driven method like waterfall. Agile welcomes change and adjusts the plan as feedback arrives.
ww.An approach that ignores all customer in: Agile relies heavily on customer input and collaboration throughout the project. Ignoring customers until the work is done is the opposite of the agile approach.
ww.An approach that avoids teamwork and has: Agile emphasizes teamwork, daily communication and shared ownership in self-organizing teams. Having each person work alone goes against its principles.

rw: A sprint is a short, fixed period, often one to four weeks, in which a team completes a set of work. Each sprint produces a usable increment that can be reviewed with the client.

ww.A race between two project teams to fini: A race between teams is not an agile practice. A sprint is a fixed work period for one team to complete agreed work, and teams collaborate rather than compete.
ww.A meeting to assign blame for delays, he: Assigning blame is not the purpose of any sprint event. Retrospectives look at how to improve the process, and a sprint is a work period, not a meeting.
ww.A final presentation to the client at th: A final client presentation at the end of the project is a closing activity. A sprint is a short repeating cycle, and each sprint ends with a review of finished work.

rw: Agile uses short cycles, such as two-week sprints, regular reviews with the client and plan adjustments. This lets the team respond to feedback and changing needs.

ww.Lean: Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow, and does not by itself define fixed two-week cycles with client reviews. The described cycles, feedback and plan changes match agile.
ww.Pricing: Pricing is a marketing decision about what to charge, not a project management method. It has nothing to do with planning work in cycles.
ww.Waterfall: Waterfall completes each phase fully before the next begins, with no repeated cycles. Reviewing with the client and adjusting the plan every two weeks is not how waterfall works.

rw: Waterfall is a sequential approach where each phase, such as requirements, design, build and test, finishes before the next one starts. It works best when requirements are clear and stable.

ww.An approach that repeats short cycles of: Short cycles with frequent customer feedback describe agile, not waterfall. Waterfall moves in a fixed sequence of phases with little feedback until later stages.
ww.An approach used only for water projects: Waterfall is a project management method used in many industries such as software, construction and manufacturing. Its name comes from work flowing downward through phases, not water.
ww.An approach that has no planning and whe: Waterfall depends on detailed planning at the start and works as a team across clearly defined phases. It does not mean having no planning or working alone.

rw: A bridge built from fixed plans has clear requirements, safety rules and a set sequence of steps. Waterfall fits because design must be complete before construction, and changes are costly.

ww.Testing a market with unknown needs: Testing a market with unknown needs calls for flexible, iterative learning, which suits agile. Waterfall needs requirements to be known up front, and here they are not.
ww.Building an app with unclear features: An app with unclear features will probably change as it is built and tested. Waterfall is a poor fit because it resists changes once a phase is complete.
ww.Testing a new idea with rapid changes: Testing a new idea with rapid changes needs quick iteration and feedback. That is the strength of agile methods, while waterfall is too rigid for it.

rw: A WBS breaks the total project scope into smaller, manageable work packages. This makes tasks easier to assign, estimate, schedule and track toward the final deliverable.

ww.A rule that limits team size and the hou: A rule limiting team size and hours is a staffing policy or constraint. A work breakdown structure divides the project's work into smaller tasks, not the people.
ww.A list of reasons a project failed, writ: A list of reasons a project failed is a post-project review or lessons learned report. A WBS is a planning tool used before and during the work.
ww.A chart of the company's profits by mont: A chart of profits by month is a financial report. A WBS shows how project work is divided and organized, not company earnings.

rw: Smaller tasks are easier to assign to people, track against the schedule and estimate for time and cost. This improves control and makes problems easier to spot early.

ww.It hides the project from stakeholders a: Breaking work down makes the project clearer to stakeholders, not hidden. It supports reporting by showing exactly what work must be completed.
ww.It makes the project take longer on purp: The goal is better control, not delay. Smaller tasks help teams estimate accurately and finish on time, and they do not make the project slower on purpose.
ww.It removes the need for a schedule and a: Task breakdown supports the schedule and budget, since each task can be given time and cost estimates. It does not remove the need for either.

rw: A dependency means one task cannot start or finish until another task starts or finishes. For example, you cannot test software before it is built, so the schedule must reflect the order.

ww.A team member who depends on the manager: A team member who relies on the manager for pay is an employment relationship. A project dependency links tasks, not people, and describes the order in which work must happen.
ww.A client who depends on a single product: A client relying on one product from the firm is a customer relationship. Project dependencies concern relationships between tasks inside a project plan.
ww.A cost that depends on exchange rates be: A cost that depends on exchange rates is a financial risk or assumption. A project dependency links tasks, so one cannot start or end until another does.

rw: Painting needs the wall to be built first, so one task depends on another. This is a finish-to-start dependency, a common type of task dependency in project schedules.

ww.A budget variance: A budget variance is the difference between planned and actual cost. The wall and paint example concerns the order of tasks, not money.
ww.A quality audit: A quality audit checks whether processes and results meet standards. It does not describe the link between building and painting a wall.
ww.A team conflict: A team conflict is a disagreement between people. Painting waiting on construction is a logical sequence between tasks, not a dispute.

rw: Financial information is data about a business's money, such as income, expenses, assets and liabilities. Owners, lenders and managers use it to make decisions and judge performance.

ww.Data about a business's employee birthda: Employee birthdays and anniversaries are HR information. Financial information concerns a business's money, such as income, costs, assets and debts.
ww.Data about a business's advertising colo: Advertising colors, logos and packaging are marketing and branding information, not financial data. Financial information records and reports a business's money.
ww.Data about a business's office layout an: Office layout and desk positions are facilities information. Financial information concerns money, such as revenue, costs and what the business owns and owes.

rw: An income statement reports revenue, expenses and resulting profit or loss over a period such as a month or year. It shows how profitable operations were during that time.

ww.A report of cash movements by activity f: Cash movements by activity are shown on the statement of cash flows. The income statement reports revenue, expenses and profit, which are not always the same as cash.
ww.A report of assets, liabilities and equi: Assets, liabilities and equity at one date are shown on the balance sheet. The income statement covers a period of time rather than a single date.
ww.A report of changes in owners' equity ov: Changes in owners' equity over a period are shown on the statement of owner's equity. The income statement reports profit, which is one input to that statement.

rw: A balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. It follows the accounting equation, assets equal liabilities plus equity, and shows financial position on that date.

ww.A report listing a company's customers a: A list of customers and what they buy is a sales or customer record. A balance sheet reports what the company owns, owes and its owners' stake.
ww.A report of cash in and out during a giv: Cash in and out over a period is shown on the cash flow statement. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date, not a record of movement.
ww.A report of revenue and expenses over a: Revenue and expenses over a year are shown on the income statement. The balance sheet shows financial position on a single date rather than results over time.

rw: The cash flow statement reports cash coming in and going out during a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities. It shows whether the business can pay its bills.

ww.A report of assets and liabilities on on: Assets and liabilities on one date are reported on the balance sheet. The cash flow statement covers cash movements over a period, not a snapshot of position.
ww.A report of a company's future sales goa: Future sales goals and plans belong in a sales forecast or budget. A cash flow statement reports actual cash received and paid in a past period.
ww.A report of profit after taxes for the w: Profit after taxes is reported on the income statement. The cash flow statement tracks cash, and profit can differ from cash because of credit sales and non-cash costs.

rw: The cash flow statement shows cash received and paid. High profit with little cash can happen when sales are on credit, inventory is growing, or large loan payments and purchases use cash.

ww.A customer survey form: A customer survey form gathers opinions and has no financial data. It cannot explain why a profitable company is short of cash.
ww.The mission statement: A mission statement describes purpose and values, and contains no figures. It cannot show where a company's cash went.
ww.A marketing plan sheet: A marketing plan sheet outlines promotion strategy and has no cash records. It cannot explain a gap between profit and cash.

rw: The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + owner's equity. It must always balance, because everything a business owns is financed by debt or by the owners.

ww.Assets equal revenue minus all the expen: Assets minus expenses is not the accounting equation. Revenue minus expenses gives net income, and assets are balanced against liabilities and equity.
ww.Equity equals debts minus revenue each y: Equity equals assets minus liabilities, not debts minus revenue. Revenue does not appear in the basic accounting equation at all.
ww.Liabilities equal assets plus owner's eq: This reverses the equation. Liabilities equal assets minus owner's equity, since liabilities are what is left of assets after the owners' share is removed.

rw: Equity = assets - liabilities = $90,000 - $35,000 = $55,000. This is the owners' claim on the business after debts are paid.

ww.$35,000: $35,000 is the liabilities figure itself, not equity. Equity is assets minus liabilities, so the owners' share is $90,000 - $35,000.
ww.$90,000: $90,000 is total assets, not equity. Part of those assets is financed by $35,000 of liabilities, leaving less for the owners.
ww.$125,000: $125,000 results from adding assets and liabilities together. The equation is subtraction: $90,000 - $35,000 = $55,000 of equity.

rw: Double-entry bookkeeping records each transaction in at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits. This keeps the accounting equation balanced and helps catch errors.

ww.Recording only cash sales and ignoring a: Double-entry does not mean ignoring credit sales. It records all transactions, including credit sales, with equal debits and credits in at least two accounts.
ww.Recording each transaction on two differ: The word double refers to two accounts, not two days. Each transaction is recorded once in the books, with two or more equal and opposite entries.
ww.Recording each transaction by two people: Double refers to the two sides of an entry, not two people. One person can record a transaction with a debit in one account and a credit in another.

rw: A trial balance lists all ledger account balances and checks that total debits equal total credits. If they differ, there is an error to find before preparing statements.

ww.A statement of expected profits for the: Expected profits for the coming year are in a budget or forecast. A trial balance lists existing account balances to check that the books are in balance.
ww.A review of employees' performance and p: Employee performance reviews are an HR activity. A trial balance is an accounting check on ledger totals, not a review of staff.
ww.A test of a new product with customers t: Testing a new product with customers is market testing. A trial balance is an accounting list of balances and has no link to customer demand.

rw: A budget is a plan estimating income and expenses for a future period. Managers compare actual results with it to control spending and spot problems.

ww.A record of past transactions made by a: A record of past transactions is a ledger or journal. A budget looks forward, planning expected income and spending rather than recording what has happened.
ww.A report of competitors' prices, compile: A report on competitors' prices is market research. A budget is an internal financial plan for the business's own income and expenses.
ww.A list of owners and partners and the sh: A list of owners and the shares they hold is a shareholder or ownership register. A budget plans money, not ownership.

rw: Variance = actual - budget = $23,500 - $20,000 = $3,500. Spending above the budget is an unfavorable variance, so the department is $3,500 over budget.

ww.$0 over budget: A $0 variance means actual spending matched the budget. Here spending of $23,500 exceeded the $20,000 budget, so there is a variance.
ww.$43,500 over budget: $43,500 adds budget and actual together. Variance is the difference between them, not the sum, so it should be $23,500 - $20,000.
ww.$3,500 under budget: The amount of $3,500 is right, but spending $23,500 against a $20,000 budget is over, not under. Under budget would mean actual spending was lower than $20,000.

rw: Accounts receivable is money owed to a business by customers who bought on credit. It is a current asset because the business expects to collect the cash soon.

ww.Cash held in a bank account by the busin: Cash held in a bank account is recorded as cash, not receivables. Receivables are amounts customers still owe and have not yet paid.
ww.Money a business owes to suppliers for g: Money owed to suppliers for goods bought is accounts payable, which is a liability. Receivable is the opposite, money owed to the business.
ww.Money the owner invests in the business: Money the owner invests is owner's equity or capital. Accounts receivable arises when customers buy on credit and owe the business.

rw: Accounts payable is money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services bought on credit. It is a current liability that must be paid by the due date.

ww.Money customers owe a business for sales: Money customers owe a business is accounts receivable, an asset. Accounts payable is the opposite, an amount the business itself owes.
ww.Money earned from sales made to customer: Money earned from sales is revenue. Accounts payable relates to purchases made on credit, not income earned from customers.
ww.Money the business holds as cash in its: Cash in the bank is an asset. Accounts payable is a liability showing what the business owes its suppliers.

rw: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average receivables = $240,000 / $30,000 = 8 times. The firm collects its average receivables about eight times a year.

ww.270 times: 270 times adds the sales and receivables together. Turnover divides net credit sales by average receivables, so the result is far smaller.
ww.0.125 times: 0.125 inverts the formula: $30,000 / $240,000. Turnover puts credit sales on top, so the correct ratio is $240,000 / $30,000 = 8.
ww.210 times: 210 times comes from subtracting $30,000 from $240,000. Turnover is a division, so $240,000 / $30,000 = 8 times, not 210.

rw: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures liquidity, or the ability to pay short-term debts with assets that convert to cash within a year.

ww.Sales divided by inventory held at year: Sales divided by inventory is the inventory turnover ratio, which shows how fast stock sells. The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities.
ww.Total liabilities divided by total asset: Total liabilities divided by total assets is the debt ratio, which measures leverage. The current ratio looks only at short-term assets and short-term obligations.
ww.Net income divided by total sales for th: Net income divided by sales is the profit margin. The current ratio measures short-term liquidity using the balance sheet.

rw: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5. The company has $1.50 of current assets for every $1 of short-term debt.

ww.20: 20 is the difference between the figures expressed in thousands ($60 - $40). The current ratio is a division, giving $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5.
ww.100: 100 is not a division result here. Current ratio = $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5, with no multiplication by 100 or use of a percentage.
ww.0.67: 0.67 inverts the ratio ($40,000 / $60,000). The current ratio puts current assets on top, so it is $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5.

rw: Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold. It shows how much the business earns from selling goods before operating expenses, interest and taxes are paid.

ww.Sales plus the cost of goods sold: Adding cost of goods sold to sales gives a meaningless total. Gross profit subtracts the cost of goods sold from sales to show what is left to cover other costs.
ww.Sales minus all expenses and taxes: Sales minus all expenses and taxes gives net income, not gross profit. Gross profit subtracts only the cost of goods sold.
ww.Assets minus all of the liabilities: Assets minus liabilities is owner's equity. Gross profit is an income statement figure based on sales and cost of goods sold.

rw: Operating profit = sales - cost of goods sold - operating expenses = $500,000 - $320,000 - $110,000 = $70,000. This is the profit from regular operations before interest and taxes.

ww.$390,000: $390,000 is sales minus operating expenses ($500,000 - $110,000), skipping the cost of goods sold. All of the costs must be subtracted from sales.
ww.$180,000: $180,000 is the gross profit ($500,000 - $320,000). Operating expenses of $110,000 must still be subtracted to reach operating profit.
ww.$930,000: $930,000 adds all three figures together. Operating profit subtracts the costs from sales, so $500,000 - $320,000 - $110,000 = $70,000.

rw: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. This matches the expense to the periods in which the asset helps earn revenue.

ww.Selling an asset for cash at the end of: Selling an asset for cash is a disposal, and any gain or loss is recorded separately. Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over the years it is used.
ww.Paying off a loan early to save interest: Paying off a loan early is debt repayment. Depreciation is the allocation of an asset's cost and has nothing to do with interest on loans.
ww.Increasing the value of an asset over ti: Depreciation decreases, not increases, the recorded value of an asset as it wears out or becomes obsolete. Assets that gain value over time are not depreciated.

rw: Straight-line depreciation = (cost - salvage value) / useful life = ($12,000 - $0) / 5 years = $2,400 per year. The same expense is recorded each year.

ww.$12,000: $12,000 is the full cost of the equipment, which would be expensed in one year. Straight-line depreciation divides the cost over its 5-year life.
ww.$60,000: $60,000 multiplies cost by the years ($12,000 x 5). Depreciation divides the cost by the useful life: $12,000 / 5 = $2,400.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 divides by 10 rather than 5. The equipment lasts 5 years, so the yearly expense is $12,000 / 5 = $2,400.

rw: Financial forecasting estimates future revenues, costs and cash needs using past data and expected trends. Managers use forecasts to plan budgets, financing and investments.

ww.Recording past sales in a ledger at day: Recording past sales in a ledger is bookkeeping, which looks backward. Forecasting looks ahead to estimate what revenues, costs and cash needs are likely to be.
ww.Counting inventory at year end in the wa: Counting inventory at year end is a stocktake, which verifies what is on hand now. Forecasting estimates future financial results.
ww.Printing a financial statement for the f: Printing a statement for the file is record keeping. Forecasting involves analyzing and predicting future results, not producing copies of past reports.

rw: Lenders review income, assets, debts and cash flow to judge whether the business can repay a loan with interest. Strong statements improve the chance of approval and better terms.

ww.To set the opening hours and staff on ea: Opening hours and shift staffing are operational scheduling decisions. Lenders use financial statements to measure a borrower's finances, not to set work schedules.
ww.To choose the business's logo and its co: A logo and its colors are branding choices. A lender does not need financial statements for that, but for judging a borrower's financial strength.
ww.To set the business's prices for the nex: Prices are set by the business, not by lenders. Lenders read statements to assess risk, not to decide what the borrower charges customers.

rw: An audit is an independent examination of financial records and statements. Auditors check accuracy and compliance with accounting rules, which adds credibility for owners and lenders.

ww.A forecast of profits for the coming yea: A forecast of coming profits is a projection. An audit examines records of what has already happened to check they are accurate and fair.
ww.A daily entry of transactions in the sal: Daily entry of transactions is bookkeeping, done by the firm's staff. An audit is a separate review by an independent person.
ww.A sales meeting to talk about prices and: A sales meeting about prices is a commercial discussion. An audit is a review of financial records for accuracy, not a negotiation.

rw: GAAP means Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, a common set of rules and standards for recording and reporting financial information. In the US, FASB sets them for public companies.

ww.A schedule of employee pay dates and the: A schedule of pay dates is a payroll calendar. GAAP stands for Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the standard rules for preparing financial statements.
ww.A federal program for small businesses t: A federal grants program is not GAAP. GAAP is a body of accounting standards, and no money is given out under it.
ww.A tax on corporate profit that large fir: A tax on corporate profit is income tax, set by tax law. GAAP is a set of accounting rules and is not a tax.

rw: Consistent rules make statements comparable between periods and between firms, and reliable for owners, lenders and investors. Common standards build trust in reported numbers.

ww.So that taxes are never paid by the firm: Accounting rules do not remove taxes. Businesses still owe tax based on tax law, and accurate records are needed to figure out the correct amount.
ww.So that every business reports the same: Firms with different results will still report different profits. Consistent rules only make sure that the figures are measured in the same way.
ww.So that accounting is easier to ignore f: Rules exist to make accounting reliable and comparable, so it cannot be ignored. Following them is required for audits, loans and, for public firms, SEC filings.

rw: Financial ratios compare figures, such as current assets to current liabilities, to judge performance, liquidity and financial health. They let users compare across periods and against competitors.

ww.Printing receipts for customers at the f: Receipts are printed by a point-of-sale system. A financial ratio compares figures from the statements to evaluate how the business is doing.
ww.Choosing a company slogan for the next a: A slogan is a marketing decision. Ratios are analytical tools built from financial statement numbers, and they play no part in choosing slogans.
ww.Scheduling employee shifts for the comin: Scheduling shifts is a staffing task. Financial ratios are calculated from financial data to assess profitability, liquidity and debt levels.

rw: Profit margin = net income / sales = $24,000 / $300,000 = 0.08, or 8%. The business keeps 8 cents of profit from each dollar of sales.

ww.80%: 80% would mean profit was almost all of sales. $24,000 / $300,000 is 0.08, so the correct margin is 8%, not 80%.
ww.0.8%: 0.8% is off by a factor of ten. $24,000 / $300,000 = 0.08, which is 8% as a percentage.
ww.12.5%: 12.5% is the result of dividing $300,000 by $24,000 incorrectly (1/8). Margin puts net income on top: $24,000 / $300,000 = 8%.

rw: Data integrity is the accuracy, completeness and consistency of financial data over its life. Controls, validation and audit trails protect it from errors and unauthorized changes.

ww.Hiding data from auditors and from the s: Hiding data from auditors and tax authorities is fraud and violates the law. Data integrity means the data stay accurate and reliable.
ww.Storing data in many different formats s: Storing data in many formats creates inconsistency and errors. Integrity depends on controlled, consistent data that stay correct.
ww.Deleting data at random from the system: Random deletion destroys records and would break integrity. Records must be retained for the required period, and deleted only under a proper retention policy.

rw: Role-based access limits changes to authorized people, and an audit trail records who changed what and when. Together they prevent and detect unauthorized changes to financial data.

ww.Sharing one password among all staff: Sharing one password removes accountability, because no one can tell who made a change. It makes unauthorized changes easier and harder to trace.
ww.Turning off all system activity logging: Turning off logging removes the record of who did what, which makes unauthorized changes undetectable. Logs are a key control for financial data.
ww.Allowing anyone to edit any record: Letting anyone edit any record invites errors and fraud. Good control limits who can change data, based on duties.

rw: A knowledge audit identifies what knowledge an organization has, where it is stored and where gaps or risks exist. The findings guide training, documentation and knowledge sharing.

ww.A review of a firm's yearly tax payments: A review of tax payments is a tax or accounting review. A knowledge audit looks at knowledge assets such as skills, documents and expertise, not taxes.
ww.A review of customers' complaints about: Reviewing customer complaints about prices is a customer feedback analysis. A knowledge audit examines what the organization knows internally and where it is missing.
ww.A review of the number of computers in t: Counting computers is an inventory of equipment. A knowledge audit studies knowledge held in people, processes and documents, not hardware numbers.

rw: Documenting the process and training a second person spreads the knowledge, so work continues if the expert is absent or leaves. This reduces the risk of relying on one employee.

ww.Keep the process secret to protect the w: Keeping the process secret creates a risk for the company and does not protect anyone. If that worker is absent or leaves, production stops with no one able to run the machine.
ww.Wait until the worker leaves before acti: Waiting until the worker leaves is too late, because the knowledge would be lost with them. Knowledge transfer should be planned in advance.
ww.Ban anyone else from touching the machin: Banning others from the machine guarantees the knowledge stays in one person. It increases risk and does not help the business continue if that person is gone.

rw: Institutional memory is the shared knowledge, history, practices and lessons an organization has built up over time. It helps new staff learn why things are done a certain way.

ww.A single employee's personal diary of wh: One employee's personal diary is individual knowledge, not the collective memory of the organization. Institutional memory is shared across many people and records.
ww.A list of past customers' addresses held: A list of past customers is a customer record. Institutional memory covers organizational know-how and history, not just contact data.
ww.The computer storage in a company's serv: Server storage is a hardware tool that may hold files. Institutional memory is the knowledge itself, held by people, processes and records.

rw: A document management system stores, organizes, tracks and controls access to documents, often with search and version control. It keeps files secure and easy to find.

ww.A machine that prints documents faster t: Printing is just one use of documents, and a faster printer is hardware. A document management system is software for managing files, not a printing machine.
ww.A tool that sets employee schedules for: Setting employee schedules is done by scheduling software. A document management system organizes documents, not work hours.
ww.A rule that bans paper in an office and: A paperless policy is a rule, not a system. A document management system is software that stores and manages documents, whether scanned or created digitally.

rw: Version control shows which version is current, records changes, and lets teams recover earlier versions. It prevents confusion and lost work when several people edit the same document.

ww.It deletes all earlier versions so only: Version control keeps earlier versions so they can be recovered. Deleting them would remove its main benefit and risk losing useful information.
ww.It makes documents impossible to edit fo: Version control does not lock documents from editing. It allows many users to edit while tracking each change.
ww.It hides who made changes and when they: Version control records who changed a file and when, which makes changes visible and accountable. Hiding them would defeat its purpose.

rw: An FAQ page lists common questions with clear answers so people can quickly find help. It reduces calls to support staff and improves the customer experience.

ww.Advertising unrelated products to the cu: Advertising unrelated products is not the purpose of an FAQ. An FAQ page helps customers by answering questions they commonly ask about the product or service.
ww.Collecting customers' credit card number: Collecting credit card numbers is a payment function and would be risky on an FAQ page. An FAQ shares information and does not gather sensitive data.
ww.Listing every employee's salary for all: Publishing salaries is not an FAQ function and would breach privacy. FAQs answer common questions about products, services or policies.

rw: Training documentation is written guides, manuals or step-by-step instructions that teach employees how to do tasks. It helps new hires learn consistently and preserves knowledge.

ww.A list of tasks that staff must avoid do: A list of tasks to avoid is a prohibition list. Training documentation teaches people how to do their jobs correctly, with steps, examples and standards.
ww.A report of the firm's yearly profit and: A report of yearly profit and costs is a financial statement. Training documentation is educational material for employees, not a record of results.
ww.A schedule of company holidays for the w: A holiday schedule is an HR calendar. Training documentation explains job procedures, not when the office is closed.

rw: A clear onboarding guide answers common setup questions once and is reusable for every new hire. It saves staff time, speeds up training and is a lasting fix.

ww.Hire fewer new workers in the coming yea: Hiring fewer workers does not solve the problem and may hurt growth. The repeated questions show a lack of written guidance that should be provided.
ww.Tell them to stop asking questions so st: Telling people to stop asking prevents them from learning and causes errors. Staff should be given the answers in a lasting form instead.
ww.Remove all written instructions from the: Removing written instructions makes the problem worse, because new hires have nowhere to look for answers. Good documentation reduces repeated questions.

rw: A data governance policy sets rules for how an organization collects, stores, protects and uses data. It assigns responsibilities and supports quality, privacy and legal compliance.

ww.A schedule of backup tapes only, kept by: A schedule of backup tapes is a narrow IT task. A data governance policy covers how all data are collected, stored, used, secured and shared.
ww.A rule that sets product prices in the s: Setting prices is a marketing or management decision. Data governance concerns the management and control of the organization's data.
ww.A list of the firm's competitors and the: A competitor price list is market research. Data governance concerns the organization's own handling of data, not tracking rivals.

rw: Job shadowing means following an experienced worker to see how tasks are done and why. It transfers practical knowledge, such as judgment and tips, that manuals may miss.

ww.Replacing a worker for a week with no he: Replacing a worker with no help is a sink-or-swim approach. Job shadowing involves observation and guidance from someone experienced, not being left alone.
ww.Reading a manual alone with no practice: Reading a manual alone with no practice is self-study, not shadowing. Shadowing requires watching and learning from a person doing the job.
ww.Watching a video of an unrelated industr: Watching a video from an unrelated industry has no link to the job. Shadowing is observing a real colleague doing the work you need to learn.

rw: Mentoring and working side by side lets learners watch, ask questions and practice with feedback. This is the best way to pass on tacit skills that cannot be fully written down.

ww.Emailing a long list of rules to them: Emailing a long list of rules works for explicit knowledge that is easily written down. Hard-to-document skills are tacit and need personal demonstration and practice.
ww.Posting a single notice on a wall: A single wall notice is a one-way message that cannot transfer subtle skills. Tacit skills are learned through interaction and observation.
ww.Restricting access to the expert: Restricting access to the expert prevents anyone from learning from them, so the skills stay locked in one person. Sharing needs closer contact, not less.

rw: To curate information is to select, organize and maintain the most useful and accurate material. Curation keeps knowledge relevant, trustworthy and easy to find.

ww.To hide information from all staff and t: Hiding information from staff is the opposite of curation. Curation makes the right information available and useful to the people who need it.
ww.To collect every document without checki: Collecting everything without checking is hoarding, not curation. Curation involves judging quality and relevance, which keeps out outdated or wrong material.
ww.To delete information at random from the: Random deletion removes valuable information and has no quality test. Curation removes only material that is outdated, duplicated or inaccurate.

rw: Reviewing, organizing and removing or archiving outdated files keeps useful information easy to find and avoids losing records. It also reduces confusion and storage costs.

ww.Add more duplicate files to the shared d: Adding more duplicates makes the clutter worse and makes it harder to find the right file. The drive needs cleanup, not more files.
ww.Delete every file at once without checki: Deleting everything at once without checking risks losing important records. Files should be reviewed first, and some may be needed for legal or business reasons.
ww.Tell staff to avoid the drive and use pe: Avoiding the shared drive moves information to private folders where others cannot find it. This fragments knowledge and creates new problems.

rw: A quality circle is a small group of employees who meet regularly to identify, analyze and solve quality problems in their work area. It uses worker knowledge and builds involvement.

ww.A circle drawn on a chart of sales to ma: A circle drawn on a sales chart is only a chart marking. A quality circle is a group of employees who meet to solve work-related quality problems.
ww.A group of customers who test prices and: Testing prices with customers is market research. A quality circle is made up of employees and focuses on improving quality in processes.
ww.A meeting held to assign blame for mista: Quality circles are for problem solving, not assigning blame. Blame discourages honest reporting, which would defeat the circle's purpose.

rw: A weekly meeting of workers to find ways to cut defects is the definition of a quality circle. It uses employees' own knowledge to improve the process.

ww.A fierce price war: A price war is competition among sellers cutting prices. It has nothing to do with workers meeting to reduce defects.
ww.A franchise deal: A franchise deal is a business arrangement to license a brand. It does not describe an employee group focused on quality.
ww.A tariff on imports: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It has no relation to employees working together on quality.

rw: A control chart tracks a process over time against upper and lower limits. Points outside the limits, or unusual patterns, signal a problem that needs investigation.

ww.Listing employees' names and their pay r: A list of names and pay rates is a payroll record. A control chart plots process data over time against control limits to show whether a process is stable.
ww.Choosing the color of a product and the: Choosing color and package shape is product design. A control chart is a statistical quality tool for monitoring how a process performs.
ww.Setting the price of a product that is s: Setting price is a marketing decision. A control chart tracks quality data, not prices.

rw: A Pareto chart rests on the 80/20 idea that a few causes produce most of the problems. It ranks causes so a team can fix the vital few first for the biggest gain.

ww.The idea that problems solve themselves: A Pareto chart assumes problems do not solve themselves, and ignoring them lets them continue. It identifies which causes should be fixed first.
ww.The idea that price alone decides qualit: Price alone does not decide quality. The Pareto chart ranks causes of problems by how often they occur.
ww.The idea that all causes of a problem ar: The Pareto principle says causes are not equal. A small number of them produce most of the effects, which is why they are ranked by size.

rw: Pareto analysis says to focus on the few causes producing most problems. Fixing those two causes, which account for 80 percent of defects, gives the largest improvement for the effort.

ww.Stop measuring defects at all: Stopping defect measurement would remove the data needed to improve. Measurement should continue to show whether fixes work.
ww.Ignore both and fix the rest: Ignoring the two causes leaves 80 percent of defects in place. Effort should go to the vital few causes, not the minor remaining ones.
ww.Spread effort evenly across all: Spreading effort evenly wastes resources on minor causes. Pareto analysis directs resources to the biggest causes first.

rw: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem into categories, such as people, methods, machines and materials. It helps a team find the root cause.

ww.Mapping the path of a delivery truck thr: Mapping a truck route is route planning, done with maps or logistics software. A fishbone diagram organizes causes of a problem.
ww.Listing the steps of a sale made in a sh: Listing the steps of a sale describes a flowchart or process map. A fishbone diagram groups possible causes of one problem.
ww.Showing a company's profit by month in t: Profit by month is shown on a financial chart or line graph. A fishbone diagram is a quality tool for cause analysis, not a financial report.

rw: A customer requirement is a need or expectation that a product or service must meet. Quality is measured by how well the product satisfies those requirements.

ww.A list of competitors' prices for the sa: Competitor prices are market data. A customer requirement is a need or expectation that the product or service must satisfy to be considered good quality.
ww.A rule that customers must follow when t: A rule for shoppers in a store is a store policy. A customer requirement describes what customers need from the product or service.
ww.A fee customers pay for service at a sho: A fee paid for service is a price or charge. A customer requirement is a need that the business must meet, and not a payment.

rw: Measuring the crashes and finding the cause is the first step in quality improvement. Data show how often the app fails and why, so the right fix can be chosen.

ww.Hide the complaints from the rest of the: Hiding complaints stops the team from learning about the problem. Quality improvement depends on using customer feedback.
ww.Raise the price of the app for all users: Raising the price does not fix crashes and may drive customers away. The cause of the crashes must be found and corrected.
ww.Remove customer support for the app's us: Removing support leaves users with no help and does not fix the crashes. It would worsen customer satisfaction.

rw: A service guarantee is a promise to fix the problem or refund the customer if a service does not meet stated standards. It reduces customer risk and builds trust.

ww.A discount for large orders placed by re: A discount for large orders is a volume discount, which is a pricing tool. A service guarantee is a promise about service quality.
ww.A tax on services that firms must pay to: A tax on services is a government charge. A service guarantee is a business's own promise to customers.
ww.A list of services offered by the firm t: A list of services offered is a service catalog. A guarantee goes further and promises a remedy if the service falls short.

rw: A promise to refund if a package is more than a day late is a service guarantee. It commits the firm to a standard and a remedy if it fails to meet it.

ww.A price skimming plan: Price skimming sets a high price on a new product, then lowers it over time. A refund promise for late delivery is not a pricing plan.
ww.A franchise fee: A franchise fee is paid by a franchisee to use a brand. It has nothing to do with refunds for late deliveries.
ww.A reverse channel: A reverse channel moves products back from customers, as with returns or recycling. A refund promise for lateness is a quality commitment.

rw: A QMS is a set of processes, rules and responsibilities used to meet quality goals consistently. It includes documentation, measurement and continuous improvement, as in ISO 9001.

ww.A tax system for firms that sets what ea: A tax system is run by government. A quality management system is a company's own set of processes for meeting quality goals.
ww.A scoreboard of sales only, shown on a s: A sales scoreboard tracks only sales. A QMS covers processes, responsibilities and procedures across the business to deliver quality.
ww.A computer game for employees that tests: A skills game for lunch is not a QMS. A QMS is a formal system, such as the ISO 9001 framework, used to manage quality.

rw: Quality depends on everyone in the organization, not just inspectors. Training all employees in quality methods helps them prevent problems and improve their own work.

ww.Training removes the need for any standa: Training does not remove the need for standards. Standards define what good quality is, and training teaches employees how to meet them.
ww.Training makes products cost more by law: Training does not raise product costs by law. No law requires this, and training generally improves quality and cuts the cost of defects.
ww.Only managers affect quality in the firm: Quality is affected by every employee, not only managers. Workers on the line often see the problems first, so they need quality skills.

rw: Supplier quality management means working with suppliers to ensure the materials and services they provide meet quality standards. Good inputs lead to good finished products.

ww.Choosing suppliers at random without che: Choosing suppliers at random without checking quality is the opposite of managing it. Careful selection and review reduce defects and delays.
ww.Raising prices on customers who buy the: Raising prices on customers is a pricing decision. Supplier quality management concerns the quality of inputs coming from suppliers.
ww.Ignoring supplier performance until a pr: Ignoring supplier performance until sales suffer is reactive. Managing supplier quality involves monitoring performance before problems reach customers.

rw: Setting quality requirements and reviewing the supplier's performance attacks the root cause. The bakery can inspect deliveries, reject poor flour or switch suppliers if quality does not improve.

ww.Keep buying the same flour and hope the: Buying the same flour and hoping for better results does not solve the problem. Without new requirements or checks, the cakes will keep failing.
ww.Stop baking cakes and sell the oven to a: Stopping baking and selling the oven is an extreme step that gives up the business. A better fix is to address the supplier problem.
ww.Blame customers for complaints about the: Blaming customers does not address the cause, which is the poor flour. It also harms the bakery's reputation and sales.

rw: A risk register lists identified risks with their likelihood, impact, owners and response plans. Teams review it regularly so risks stay under control.

ww.A list of products on sale in the shops: A list of products on sale is a price or inventory list. A risk register records possible risks and how they will be handled.
ww.A list of employees' vacation days kept: Vacation days are HR records. A risk register tracks threats to the project or business, not staff leave.
ww.A list of customers who pay late or do n: A list of late-paying customers is a credit control report. A risk register covers all kinds of risks and their handling, not one customer group.

rw: Listing possible problems, rating them and assigning owners is maintaining a risk register. It helps the team prioritize and respond to the most serious risks.

ww.Setting a retail price list: A retail price list sets selling prices. Rating possible problems and assigning owners is risk management, not pricing.
ww.Choosing a supplier for it: Choosing a supplier is a purchasing decision. Listing and rating problems, then assigning owners, is risk register work.
ww.Preparing a sales campaign: Preparing a sales campaign is a marketing activity. The described steps identify and manage risks.

rw: Risk probability is the chance, or likelihood, that a risk event will happen. It is combined with impact to rank which risks need attention first.

ww.The person who is in charge of a risk: The person in charge of a risk is the risk owner. Probability describes how likely the event is to happen.
ww.The date a risk was first listed in the: The date a risk was listed is just a log entry. Probability measures likelihood, not timing of the entry.
ww.The cost of fixing a risk event later: The cost of fixing a risk event is part of its impact. Probability measures how likely the risk is, not how costly it is.

rw: Risk impact is the size of the loss or harm if a risk event happens, such as cost, delay or damage. Impact is rated along with probability to prioritize risks.

ww.The list of insurance policies owned by: The insurance policies a firm owns are risk responses, and not impact. Impact is the size of the possible loss.
ww.The name of the person who first found t: The name of the finder is a record detail. Impact measures how serious the consequences would be.
ww.The chance that the event will occur in: The chance of the event occurring in a year is probability. Impact measures the size of the consequences, not their likelihood.

rw: Rare but severe risks are managed by transferring the loss through insurance and reducing it through prevention, such as sprinklers and safety checks. This limits the damage if it does happen.

ww.It is ignored because it is unlikely: Ignoring a risk because it is unlikely is dangerous when the impact would be severe. A factory fire could end the business, so it needs a response.
ww.It is accepted with no plan at all: Accepting with no plan leaves the firm exposed to a very large loss. High-impact risks need planned responses even when unlikely.
ww.It is avoided by closing the business: Closing the business to avoid a fire is an extreme response that destroys the firm to avoid a small chance. Insurance and prevention are more practical.

rw: A business continuity plan explains how key operations will keep running, or be restored quickly, during a crisis. It covers people, sites, systems and suppliers to limit losses.

ww.A plan to hire more staff in the summer: Hiring summer staff is a staffing plan. A business continuity plan keeps key operations running during and after a crisis.
ww.A plan to raise prices every year on all: Raising prices is a pricing plan. A continuity plan prepares for disruptions such as fires, storms or system failures.
ww.A plan to change the company's logo and: Changing the logo is a branding plan. A continuity plan deals with keeping the business working during a crisis.

rw: Keeping off-site backups and a backup power source helps the store keep operating after a disruption. This is business continuity planning.

ww.Price discrimination by a firm: Price discrimination is charging different prices to different buyers. Off-site backups and backup power protect operations, not pricing.
ww.Market segmentation tasks: Market segmentation divides customers into groups. Backing up records and power has nothing to do with customer groups.
ww.Channel conflict between firms: Channel conflict is a dispute among distribution partners. Backups and standby power are protective measures against disruptions.

rw: A disaster recovery plan sets steps to restore systems, data and facilities after a major disruption such as a fire, flood or cyberattack. It sets recovery priorities and time targets.

ww.Steps to lower prices when a firm has to: Lowering prices to clear excess stock is a sales tactic. A disaster recovery plan restores systems and data after a major disruption.
ww.Steps to start a new product line in the: Starting a new product line is a growth strategy. A disaster recovery plan deals with restoring operations after something goes wrong.
ww.Steps to hire an employee for the firm's: Hiring an employee is a staffing task. Disaster recovery focuses on recovering technology, data and facilities after a disaster.

rw: Workplace safety training teaches employees how to avoid accidents, handle equipment correctly and respond to hazards and emergencies. It reduces injuries and supports OSHA compliance.

ww.Teaching employees to avoid reports of a: Avoiding reports would hide problems. Safety training encourages reporting of hazards and incidents so they can be fixed.
ww.Teaching employees to raise prices on al: Raising prices is a pricing decision and is unrelated to workplace safety. Training aims to protect employees from harm.
ww.Teaching employees to ignore hazards and: Ignoring hazards puts workers in danger. Safety training teaches employees to spot hazards and act to control them.

rw: Fixing the leak removes the cause, and warnings plus prompt cleanup protect people while problems occur. This is the best way to cut slips and liability.

ww.Remove all signs and warnings from the f: Removing warning signs would increase the chance of more slips. People need signs to know a floor is wet.
ww.Ignore the incidents and wait to see wha: Ignoring repeated incidents allows injuries to continue and may lead to claims. Known hazards should be dealt with promptly.
ww.Tell staff to walk faster across the flo: Telling staff to walk faster increases the chance of slipping. It does not remove the wet floor hazard.

rw: Supply chain risk is the chance that a disruption, such as a supplier failure, strike or shipping delay, will hurt the business. Firms manage it with backup suppliers and stock.

ww.The chance that a logo will be redesigne: A logo redesign is a branding matter. Supply chain risk is about disruptions to sourcing, production and delivery.
ww.The chance that a customer will leave a: A customer review is feedback, not a supply chain event. Supply chain risk concerns the flow of materials and goods.
ww.The chance that a sale will be announced: A sale announcement is a marketing event. Supply chain risk is about problems in the flow of goods from suppliers.

rw: Adding backup suppliers in other regions spreads the risk so one port strike or local event cannot stop supply. This diversification is a standard supply chain risk response.

ww.Relying even more on the same single sup: Relying more on the same supplier increases exposure. If that supplier or its port is disrupted again, the business will be hit even harder.
ww.Ordering later each time from that suppl: Ordering later does not protect against disruption, and it could cause stockouts. The firm needs alternatives, not delay.
ww.Ignoring shipping news from overseas por: Ignoring shipping news removes warning of problems. Monitoring helps, but ignoring it does not reduce the risk.

rw: Credit risk is the chance that a customer will not pay what they owe, which causes bad debts. Firms manage it by checking credit and setting terms and limits.

ww.The chance that a product will be return: Product returns are a sales or quality risk. Credit risk is the chance that a customer fails to pay a debt owed to the business.
ww.The chance that a store will run out of: Running out of stock is an inventory risk. Credit risk concerns customers who buy on credit and fail to pay.
ww.The chance that an employee will resign: An employee resigning is a human resources risk. Credit risk concerns nonpayment by customers or borrowers.

rw: Checking a new customer's payment history before offering credit is managing credit risk. It helps predict whether the customer will pay on time.

ww.Choosing a new logo: Choosing a logo is a branding decision. Checking payment history is aimed at the risk of not being paid.
ww.Setting a product price: Setting a product price is a pricing decision. A payment history check judges whether to extend credit.
ww.Planning a promotion: Planning a promotion is a marketing activity. A payment history check is a credit risk control.

rw: Reputational risk is the chance that damage to a company's image or public trust, from scandals, poor quality or bad service, will hurt sales, hiring and relationships.

ww.The chance that prices will fall by law: Prices falling by law is a regulatory or market risk. Reputational risk is damage to the company's image and public trust.
ww.The chance that a machine will break dow: A machine breaking down is an operational risk. Reputational risk concerns how the public views the company.
ww.The chance that a delivery will arrive e: An early delivery is not a risk event at all and may please customers. Reputational risk is harm to a company's image.

rw: Hiding a safety problem and being found out damages the company's reputation and customers' trust. It can also lead to lawsuits, recalls, fines and lost sales.

ww.No effect on sales at all in the next ye: Customers who find a hidden safety problem will react strongly. Sales are likely to fall, so the effect would not be none.
ww.Higher customer loyalty in the long run: Loyalty falls after a firm hides a safety problem. Customers trust honest companies and punish deception.
ww.Lower insurance needs for the firm itsel: The firm would likely need more insurance or pay higher premiums, since the risk is greater. Lower insurance needs would not follow from hiding a safety defect.

rw: A general journal is the book of original entry where transactions are first recorded in date order. Entries are later posted to the ledger accounts.

ww.A list of account balances kept by the f: A list of account balances is a trial balance. A general journal is the book where transactions are first recorded in date order.
ww.A report of annual profit that is sent t: An annual profit report is an income statement. The general journal is a day-to-day record of individual transactions.
ww.A summary of a company's assets, made at: A summary of assets at year end is a balance sheet. The general journal lists individual transactions as they happen.

rw: Buying supplies for cash increases the Supplies asset and decreases the Cash asset by the same amount. Total assets are unchanged, so the accounting equation still balances.

ww.Revenue increases and Cash increases: Revenue is earned when goods or services are sold. Buying supplies is not a sale, so revenue does not change, and cash goes down.
ww.Cash increases and Supplies decrease: Cash decreases when the business pays for supplies, and supplies increase. This option has the directions reversed.
ww.Supplies increase and Payables decrease: Payables would increase if supplies were bought on credit. The purchase here was paid in cash, so cash decreases instead of payables.

rw: A source document is original evidence of a transaction, such as a receipt, invoice or check stub. It supports the entry in the journal and is kept for audits.

ww.A list of the company's accounts and the: A list of accounts and balances is a trial balance or ledger. A source document is the original evidence that a transaction took place.
ww.A summary of a company's yearly results: A summary of yearly results is a financial statement. Source documents are individual records of single transactions.
ww.A budget for next year that the manager: A budget is a plan for the future. A source document proves a past transaction took place.

rw: A chart of accounts is a list of all the accounts a business uses to record transactions, usually with numbers. It organizes assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses.

ww.A list of customers and their balances k: A list of customers and their balances is an accounts receivable subsidiary ledger. A chart of accounts lists every account in the accounting system.
ww.A graph of sales over time that is poste: A graph of sales is a visual report. A chart of accounts is a list of account names and numbers.
ww.A schedule of loan payments due to the b: A schedule of loan payments is an amortization schedule. A chart of accounts is a full list of the accounts and not a payment plan.

rw: In a standard chart of accounts, 1 stands for assets, 2 for liabilities, 3 for equity, 4 for revenue and 5 for expenses. This numbering helps keep accounts organized.

ww.Revenue: Revenue accounts usually begin with the number 4. Numbers beginning with 1 are generally assets in a standard chart of accounts.
ww.Expenses: Expense accounts usually start with 5 or higher. Numbers beginning with 1 are assets.
ww.Debts: Debts are liabilities, which usually start with 2 in a standard chart of accounts. Accounts beginning with 1 are assets.

rw: A bank reconciliation compares the company's cash records with the bank statement and explains differences, such as outstanding checks and deposits in transit. It finds errors and fraud.

ww.Predicting next month's cash flow for th: Predicting cash flow is a forecast. A bank reconciliation compares records for a past date to find differences.
ww.Combining two bank accounts into one to: Combining accounts is a banking change. A reconciliation compares records but does not merge any accounts.
ww.Applying for a loan from a bank to fund: Applying for a loan is a financing step. A bank reconciliation checks the accuracy of cash records.

rw: Outstanding checks have been written and recorded by the company, but have not yet cleared the bank. They are subtracted from the bank balance to find the adjusted cash balance.

ww.Interest earned: Interest earned is added to the book balance, since the bank has credited it and the company has not yet recorded it. It is not subtracted from the bank balance.
ww.Bank collections: Bank collections are added to the book balance because the bank has collected on the company's behalf. They are not subtracted from the bank balance.
ww.Deposits in transit: Deposits in transit are added to the bank statement balance, since the company recorded them but the bank has not yet. They are not subtracted.

rw: A petty cash fund is a small amount of cash kept on hand to pay minor expenses, such as postage or supplies. It is managed with an imprest system and vouchers.

ww.A fund for paying owners their yearly di: Yearly dividends to owners are paid from profits through the normal bank account. Petty cash is only for small day-to-day expenses.
ww.A large fund for buying equipment and ma: Large equipment purchases go through the bank account with approvals. A petty cash fund is deliberately small.
ww.A bank loan taken out by the business ea: A bank loan is borrowed money, a liability. Petty cash is the business's own cash set aside for small payments.

rw: An invoice is a bill from a seller that lists the goods or services sold and the amount the buyer owes. It also gives payment terms and a due date.

ww.A list of company assets and their prese: A list of assets and their value is an asset register. An invoice is a bill for goods or services sold.
ww.A request to buy goods sent by a custome: A request to buy goods sent by a buyer is a purchase order. The invoice comes from the seller after the sale.
ww.A receipt for a cash sale handed to the: A receipt acknowledges payment already made. An invoice requests payment of an amount that is still owed.

rw: The terms 2/10, net 30 mean the buyer can take a 2 percent discount by paying within 10 days. Otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days.

ww.A 10 percent discount if paid within 2 d: The numbers are reversed. The discount is 2 percent for payment within 10 days, not 10 percent within 2 days.
ww.Payment is due in 2 or 10 days, or other: The terms do not mean payment is due in 2 or 10 days. The 2 is the discount percentage, 10 is the discount period, and 30 is the final due date.
ww.A $2 fee if paid after 10 days, otherwis: The terms are not a $2 fee. The 2 is a percentage discount for early payment, not a fee for paying late.
